idiom_name: immutable record with same-type methods, imitating the JDK's BigDecimal.add / Duration.plus convention
implementation_notes: Java has no operator overloading, so the pattern is an API convention supplied by the platform's own value types: java.math.BigDecimal.add(BigDecimal) returns BigDecimal, java.time.Duration.plus(Duration) returns Duration, and LocalDate.plus(...) returns LocalDate. What replaces the classic structure is that convention applied to your own immutable record - methods whose parameters and return type are the type itself, built from the canonical fields, with validation in the compact constructor - so combination code never sees primitives. The library form is the right default; reach for a mutable accumulator only inside a tight loop, converting back to the immutable value at the boundary, and use records (Java 16+) so the value type stays cheap to declare.
pitfalls: Records do not validate automatically: without a compact constructor every closed operation can produce an instance that violates the invariant it was supposed to re-establish.

Record equality is field-based, so a normalising operation (scale, rounding) can make a + b unequal to the value built directly from the same numbers - normalise in the constructor instead of in each method.
Each operation allocates a new object; in hot accumulation loops that allocation can dominate, which is why the JDK also ships mutable builders and primitive accumulators.
Methods named add/plus with different operand types (Money.plus(long)) overload silently and reintroduce unit confusion at the call site.
